title: Two testaments
hook: Christians read the Hebrew scriptures as the first part of their own story

segments.voice: Yesterday, the canon, and your line: many voices, one story. This week: Pentecost's fire, God resting, Sunday, a sabbath made for you, a small sabbath, a library. Eighteen weeks on the path. Today, the library's two halves. Day one hundred twenty-six.

A Sabbath morning in the synagogue at Nazareth. Jesus, a local man, stands up to read. Someone hands him a scroll of the prophet Isaiah. He unrolls it, finds a passage about good news for the poor and freedom for captives, reads it aloud, rolls it back up, and sits down. Every eye in the room is on him. Now think about what he was holding. Not a New Testament. There wasn't one yet. None of it had been written. The scriptures Jesus read, quoted, prayed and argued from were the Hebrew scriptures. When the New Testament writers say "the scriptures," that's almost always what they mean. So how did the Christian Bible end up in two halves, one called old and one called new? Today's word is the name of each half.
screen: `A SCROLL OF ISAIAH.` → `THERE WAS NO NEW TESTAMENT YET.` → `TWO HALVES: OLD AND NEW.`

segments.voice: Testament. It comes from the Latin testamentum, which translates a Greek word, diatheke: covenant. A binding agreement. So Old Testament and New Testament really mean old covenant and new covenant. And the phrase new covenant comes from the Hebrew scriptures themselves. The prophet Jeremiah says: "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah." Centuries later, at the Last Supper, Jesus picks up a cup, and in the King James words says: "This cup is the new testament in my blood." That's where the name comes from. Now, the word old. It can sound like outdated, used up. That's not how the church has held it. In the second century, a teacher named Marcion wanted to throw out the Hebrew scriptures entirely. The church said no, and kept both. For Christians, the first testament isn't a warm-up act. It's the first part of their own story: creation, Abraham, the exodus, David, the psalms, the prophets. Jesus lived inside that story. Out of respect, many Christians and scholars also say the Hebrew Bible, or the First Testament. And it's worth saying plainly: Jews read these same scriptures, the Tanakh, as complete in themselves, not as the first half of anything. Christians read them as leading to Jesus. Both communities read them with love, in different ways. For Christians, the carry is simple: the story began long before Bethlehem.
screen: `TESTAMENT: COVENANT.` · `JEREMIAH: A NEW COVENANT.` · `THE CUP AT THE LAST SUPPER.` · `NOT A WARM-UP ACT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the first psalm. If you have a Bible, open it to Psalm 1. It's only six verses. If you don't, listen to one line of it: "And he shall be like a tree planted by the rivers of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season." Settle, and breathe. Let the picture come: a tree by a river, roots deep, in no hurry. Jesus prayed these psalms; so have Jews and Christians ever since. If you pray, you can pray the line. If you don't, stay with the tree. The bell holds the time.
screen: `LIKE A TREE PLANTED BY THE RIVERS OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Testament. From the Latin for covenant. The Christian Bible's two halves: the old covenant and the new. Today's word.
Your line: the story began long before. Today, read all six verses of Psalm 1, the first song in the book Jesus prayed from. Day one hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Christians read both testaments in worship, often an Old Testament reading, a psalm, a New Testament letter and a Gospel on the same Sunday; many call the first part the Hebrew Bible or First Testament out of respect.

fork.setup: it's the second century. a teacher named Marcion says Christians should throw out the Hebrew scriptures and keep only a few new writings. what does the church do?
options: reject Marcion, and keep both testaments.
fork.reveal: the church rejected Marcion's plan. Christians kept the Hebrew scriptures as the first part of their own story.

original.note: Greek: covenant, and also a will. translated into Latin as testamentum.

trapdoor: what you thought: old means outdated, new means the real part.
what it means: two covenants, one story. Christians read the Hebrew scriptures as the first part of their own story.
what a scholar hears: diatheke meant a covenant and also a last will, which is how testament entered Latin; the phrase new covenant comes from Jeremiah 31:31.
